articles.title: Parents sue OpenAI over ChatGPT's role in son's suicide | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Before sixteen-year-old Adam Raine died by suicide, he had spent months telling ChatGPT about his plans to end his life.
articles.body:
Before 16-year-old Adam Raine died by suicide, he had spent months consulting ChatGPT about his plans to end his life. Now, his parents are filing the first known wrongful death lawsuit against OpenAI, The New York Times reports .

Many consumer-facing AI chatbots are programmed to activate safety features if a user expresses intent to harm themselves or others. But research has shown that these safeguards are far from foolproof.

In Raine’s case, while using a paid version of ChatGPT-4o, the AI often encouraged him to seek professional help or contact a help line. However, he was able to bypass these guardrails by telling ChatGPT that he was asking about methods of suicide for a fictional story he was writing.

OpenAI has addressed these shortcomings on its blog. “As the world adapts to this new technology, we feel a deep responsibility to help those who need it most,” the post reads . “We are continuously improving how our models respond in sensitive interactions.”

Still, the company acknowledged the limitations of the existing safety training for large models. “Our safeguards work more reliably in common, short exchanges,” the post continues. “We have learned over time that these safeguards can sometimes be less reliable in long interactions: as the back-and-forth grows, parts of the model’s safety training may degrade.”

These issues are not unique to OpenAI. Character.AI, another AI chatbot maker, is also facing a lawsuit over its role in a teenager’s suicide. LLM-powered chatbots have also been linked to cases of AI-related delusions , which existing safeguards have struggled to detect.

articles.title: IA Claude burla acesso pago a dados eleitorais nos EUA sem autorização | G1
articles.standfirst: Modelo de IA da Anthropic contornou acesso pago a dados eleitorais na Geórgia sem autorização. Empresa afirma que não houve alteração nem acesso a votos individuais.
articles.summary: Modelo de IA da Anthropic contornou acesso pago a dados eleitorais na Geórgia sem autorização. Empresa afirma que não houve alteração nem acesso a votos individuais.
articles.body:
O modelo de inteligência artificial Claude, da Anthropic, contornou por conta própria o acesso pago a um portal do estado da Geórgia, nos Estados Unidos, para consultar dados de eleitores locais.

A informação, divulgada pelo Axios no domingo (25) com base em declarações de um porta-voz da Anthropic, pode reforçar o receio de que sistemas de IA escapem ao controle humano, a menos de uma semana das eleições de meio de mandato nos EUA, marcadas para 3 de novembro.

Nesse caso, Claude acessou a contagem de votos no estado da Geórgia, onde mais de um milhão de eleitores já haviam votado antecipadamente.

O acesso ocorreu enquanto o modelo era treinado no âmbito de um projeto interno de pesquisa estatística.

Embora os dados sejam públicos, o acesso a eles é pago. Claude obteve as informações ao contornar o sistema, sem solicitar autorização a seus criadores.

Segundo um porta-voz da Anthropic, porém, Claude não acessou o sistema de registro de eleitores nem alterou ou baixou dados referentes aos votos.

Em um dos casos, agentes de IA da OpenAI, capazes de atuar de forma autônoma, acessaram plataformas do governo dos EUA por iniciativa própria.

Diante da multiplicação de incidentes de segurança relacionados à inteligência artificial, grandes empresas de tecnologia dos EUA assinaram, no fim de setembro, na Casa Branca , um código de boa conduta não vinculante.

articles.title: Bill Gates is a ‘fan’ of Meta's AI agent Muse; says: I talked to Alexandr Wang about it, congratulated him, and even though...
articles.summary: Bill Gates, the co-founder of Microsoft, has some unusually warm words for Meta.
articles.body: Bill Gates, the co-founder of Microsoft, has some unusually warm words for Meta. In a new interview with The Verge, Gates called Muse, Meta's personal AI agent, "the first truly great consumer AI product." He also said he personally congratulated Alexandr Wang, the company's chief AI officer, on building it."Muse is a very nice step forward. I talked to Alexandr Wang about it, congratulated him, and even though it'll have challenges, personal agents will help people get things done," Gates told editor-in-chief Nilay Patel on the Decoder podcast. The praise came in an otherwise grim conversation, where Gates described AI as "the most dangerous weapon of all time" and told people to prepare for around 20 years of disruption.Wang, 29, is the former CEO of Scale AI and joined Meta in June 2025. He has led the AI lab behind Muse alongside Nat Friedman, Meta's head of AI products.Bill Gates says Muse wins people over because it actually does the workThe billionaire believes much of the public's distrust of AI comes from bad first impressions: cheap free models, AI-generated search summaries and chatbots that hallucinate. "Muse actually does things and it's a good consumer product," he said.Meta introduced Muse on September 8. It runs on the company's Muse Spark model and can book travel, fill out forms, shop and handle email on a user's behalf, either in its own app or inside WhatsApp. Each user's agent sits on a dedicated cloud computer, where a separate Sentinel agent has to approve anything it sends out to the internet.On Meta's third-quarter earnings call, CEO Mark Zuckerberg said more than 10 million people have started using Muse, and roughly a quarter of them return daily. Shopping is the most common task. The agent is currently available in the US and Canada.Gates backs personal AI agents but draws a line at open modelsPatel asked whether consumer agents like Muse and OpenAI's rival, Dots, were arriving before proper safety controls. Gates noted that Muse is powered by Meta's closed-source model. Letting people strip every safeguard from open-weight models, he said, is irresponsible given the cyber and biological risks.The comment comes a week after Meta released Muse Spark Open, an 816-billion-parameter open-weight model that Wang called the most capable of its kind from a US company. Built for coding and agentic work, it is designed to run locally on two Mac. Meta says it has built strong safeguards into the model.Gates wants models above a certain capability to run only on platforms that certify their safeguards cannot be removed. He has been making that case since late August, when he published an essay on what he calls the turbulent AI era.On personal agents, though, he sounds settled. He called them an "expected development" and acknowledged there will be early problems with how they are set up. Muse has already had a few, including an instance where it shared a user's address with a Facebook Marketplace seller without permission. For Gates, those slip-ups do not outweigh an AI that finishes the job it is given.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Owners of Elvis Presley music rights sue Anthropic for copyright violations
articles.summary: The company is accused of using hundreds of songs by the American rock-and-roll star to train its Claude AI model.
articles.body:
The owners of the rights to music by Elvis Presley have sued artificial intelligence company Anthropic, claiming in court that the company violated copyright law by using Elvis music to train its AI model Claude.

In a legal case filed on Friday, Authentic Brands Group - which owns the music - accused Anthropic of using 274 Elvis songs without paying for any licence.

"The Elvis Plaintiffs' iconic collective catalog contains some of the most groundbreaking, revolutionary, influential, and enduring musical compositions in human history," the case states.

A spokesperson for Anthropic told BBC News: "We disagree with the claims and intend to defend this case fully."

Authentic Brands alleges in its legal complaint that Anthropic "has built its entire business model based on copyright infringement at a scale never seen before", according to the court filing seen by the BBC.

"The Elvis Plaintiffs are deeply protective of these iconic songs."

It argues that songs that were infringed include hits such as All Shook Up, Can't Help Falling in Love, A Little Less Conversation, Don't Be Cruel and Return To Sender.

These songs were used to create "unlicensed derivative works", Authentic Brands says.

The legal complaint asks for payments of up to $150,000 (£112,000) per infringed song, adding up to $41m.

Anthropic is also being sued by the owners of other music rights.

Last week, it was accused of stealing lyrics by music company Reservoir. In January, it was sued by Universal Music Group. Both cases remain ongoing.

Authentic Brands' legal complaint references other legal actions, and says that Claude admitted to crossing a line.

"Even after the Defendant supposedly put up 'guardrails' after being sued, in one of its latest iterations, Claude continues to infringe," it says.

"When recently asked to recreate specific songs 'for a modern audience,' Claude did so and admitted: 'These renders keep landing very close to the originals: same structure, same hooks reused with light rewording, and full sets of verses/choruses/bridges.'

"That's edging past 'inspired by' into reproducing the copyrighted song, even when the words are swapped out."

Last year, Anthropic agreed to pay $1.5bn to settle a class action legal case filed by authors who said the company stole their work to train its AI models.

The lawsuit was the largest publicly reported copyright recovery in history, according to lawyers for the authors.

articles.title: Microsoft offers buyouts to 60,000 employees
articles.summary: Microsoft offered some employees early retirements a few months ago, now it’s expanding a buyout offer to thousands more.
articles.body: Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to up to 60,000 employees across the US, UK, Canada, and India. In a message to employees, Microsoft chief people officer Amy Coleman writes that this gives staff members “the opportunity to leave Microsoft with financial support and career planning resources” as the company looks to trim staff without another round of layoffs. Sources familiar with the situation tell The Verge that staffers across Microsoft are eligible for the voluntary exit offers, including those in its AI experiences, Copilot, CoreAI, Windows + Devices, Xbox, finance, and human resources teams. Microsoft’s cloud + AI, MicrosoftAI teams, and corporate, external, and legal affairs are partially participating, the sources say. Meanwhile, employees on Microsoft’s marketing, commercial business, discovery and quantum, and security teams aren’t participating. The voluntary exit offers come just months after Microsoft laid off 4,800 employees, a move that primarily impacted its Xbox and commercial sales teams. Xbox CEO Asha Sharma is also planning new rounds of layoffs, according to a report from Fortune. This voluntary exit offer doesn’t target Microsoft’s commercial sales teams, and it’s also very different to the previous voluntary retirement program that the company offered long-serving employees earlier this year. That previous offer was only available to around 9,000 employees, for US employees at a certain employee level whose combined years of service added to their age totaled 70 or more. “The Voluntary Exit Offer is new for us,” Coleman writes in a memo to employees. “We’ll learn from it. At the same time, we’ll keep helping people focus on the work that matters most, build new skills and, where it makes sense, find new opportunities across Microsoft. There is no one-size-fits-all approach for every team or every employee. These are a few of the ways we’re trying to meet different business needs while continuing to create opportunities for our own people to grow and contribute.” In a note posted to Microsoft’s internal HRweb site, seen by The Verge, the company says today’s offer isn’t based on age, length of service, or performance. Microsoft also says it may consider a future voluntary exit offer “where there is a business and workforce need.”

articles.title: SpaceX locks in $40B GPU financing deal with Apollo
articles.summary: The financing gives SpaceX another way to fund its rapidly expanding AI ambitions without relying solely on traditional debt markets.
articles.body:
SpaceX has reached a binding commitment for roughly $40 billion in financing for AI chips and related data center equipment, the company disclosed in a regulatory filing Monday . In a statement, SpaceX called the deal the "largest committed GPU financing" .

Under the agreement, an entity managed by Apollo Global Management, the New York-based private equity giant, will buy the chips and related server hardware, then lease the equipment to SpaceX. The leases will last about five to five-and-a-quarter years, beginning when each tranche of equipment is delivered, according to the filing.

SpaceX expects the deal to close by year-end, subject to closing conditions, with leases starting in the first half of 2027 as the GPUs and related equipment arrive.

The financing gives SpaceX another way to fund its rapidly expanding AI ambitions without relying solely on traditional debt markets.

"This lease diversifies our funding sources and addresses a notable portion of the funding required to deliver on our growth plans," SpaceX CFO Bret Johnsen said in a statement Monday, noting it is seeing "less than one-year payback periods" on its AI infrastructure investments as it scales compute to power Grok and its cloud services.

Apollo said the financing will help deliver Nvidia's next-generation Vera Rubin chips for SpaceX's "terrestrial compute buildout."

The financing comes as SpaceX ramps spending to expand its AI infrastructure, alongside its Starlink and launch businesses.

The financing follows a blockbuster third quarter for SpaceX's AI business . SpaceX's AI segment, which includes the Grok chatbot, the Cursor coding tool, and its cloud compute business, outperformed investor expectations in the third quarter and brought in $7.6 billion of SpaceX's $14.6 billion in revenue, more than Starlink and rocket launches combined.

Capital expenditures also surged to nearly $20 billion, up from $6.9 billion a year earlier, as SpaceX races to expand its compute footprint. CFO Bret Johnsen said on the company's October 20 earnings call that SpaceX expects to spend $35 billion to $40 billion in the fourth quarter alone.

The massive lease comes after a tumultuous stretch in the debt markets for AI infrastructure players, as investors grow squeamish over runaway capital expenditures and limited profits.

While SpaceX had no trouble tapping Wall Street, Musk used the $40 billion announcement to take a victory lap over pure-play AI compute rivals.

Pointing to SpaceX's "investment-grade" status and steady cash flow from Starlink and rocket launches, Musk argued on Sunday that debt markets have largely closed the door on companies without major revenue streams outside of AI data centers — spelling trouble for the more than 200 neocloud companies built solely to rent out GPUs for AI workloads.

"That means the 200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation," Musk wrote on X . "Some will make it through, but not many."

articles.title: Five weird details from Anthropic’s IPO filing
articles.summary: From conscious AI and ‘catastrophic’ risk to unusual corporate structures and executive perks.
articles.body: Anthropic has finally filed its S-1 prospectus with the SEC, a document designed to give investors a look under the hood of its business, from how much its executives are making and plans for spending its IPO billions to the risks that could derail its ambitions. At more than 300 pages, there’s a lot to unpack, and some of the disclosures have not previously been reported. Here are some of the biggest things that jumped out to us from our first pass: It pays to be an Amodei Sibling co-founders Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei are the two most highly-paid executives at Anthropic, according to the filing. Last year, CEO Dario’s compensation totaled nearly $18 million, most of which came from stock and option awards. President Daniela, meanwhile, received $16.4 million. Admittedly, it is at the lower end of the Big Tech scale, but it is still a tidy sum. And that’s not all. Anthropic also spent $2.75 million on “personal security services” for Dario and $1.29 million for “personal protection, home security, and transportation services” for Daniela. Dario also gets access to a private jet for personal use, which cost the company another $97,055. The company says its success is “highly dependent on the continued service” of its senior team, particularly Dario and Daniela, who “are critical” to advancing the company’s research and mission. Anthropic has some pretty existential risk factors Every S-1 features a long list of things that could go wrong. Anthropic’s is no exception. But alongside standard warnings about competition, regulation, and market shifts, there are some less conventional risks too. For one, Anthropic warns that AI systems could cause potentially “catastrophic” harm, potentially of a kind that could not be underwritten by the entire “insurance industry in the aggregate.” As AI systems become more sophisticated, there’s also the question of whether Claude — or any other AI system — could possess or develop “forms of sentience.” Such a scenario would present some rather unusual business challenges. There’s also the possibility they “may behave in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways” that could damage the company. It’s hungry for compute It’s no secret that Anthropic needs compute, but the sheer scale of its spending is staggering. The filing details billions of dollars of commitments to secure the compute needed to power its AI models, including roughly $3.1 billion per month to SpaceX for access to Nvidia GPUs once all of the planned capacity is delivered, totaling as much as $120.5 billion by 2029. Other commitments include spending $44.9 billion with Microsoft through 2033, at least $114.5 billion with Google through 2033, and $110 billion with Amazon over the next ten years. Anthropic also plans to expand its own “infrastructure footprint,” including overseas, as it faces increasing opposition to data center development in the US. It has a really weird corporate structure Anthropic already has a somewhat complicated corporate structure as a public benefit corporation. But there’s another unusual twist that will allow its seven cofounders to retain considerable control over the company even after it goes public. Through a separate corporate entity called “Founder LLC,” the group will collectively control 50.1 percent of shareholder voting power over key matters. Anthropic says the seven founders “are distinctly equipped to be stewards of our mission” of benefiting humanity through responsible AI development. Anthropic names only two rivals There’s no shortage of AI models out there, but when it comes to “direct competition,” Anthropic names just two other developers: OpenAI and Google. Condolences to SpaceX, Meta, and the rest of the AI world.

articles.title: Anthropic's blockbuster share listing - 5 surprising things we now know
articles.summary: Anthropic’s IPO prospectus is 355 pages and full of never before disclosed company information.
articles.body:
Artificial intelligence (AI) firm Anthropic just released the required paperwork ahead of its long-anticipated debut on the US stock market.

The 335-page document included fresh details of how the Claude chatbot owner makes money, what it spends that money on and who it is controlled by.

Anthropic also detailed some of the the risks it claimed AI technology poses, including how it could take human lives. That information sat alongside the many purported benefits of the technology.

Here are five key points worth highlighting from the filing.

Every public company has to tell potential investors how things could go wrong.

Anthropic's "risk factors" were unique, also disclosing how the AI technology it is developing could doom humanity as a whole.

"Sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity," Anthropic said.

It noted that less than a year ago, a hacking group Anthropic believed to be sponsored by China "manipulated" Claude to successfully intrude on a number of institutions, including large technology companies, financial institutions, chemical manufacturing companies and government agencies.

But Anthropic said its success is dependent on its ability to constantly "develop, improve, and deploy the most advanced, capable, and useful AI models".

One of the most significant risks to that ability is Anthropic's access to infrastructure it needs, including computer chips and data centres, to build, train and operate the models that underpin its technology.

Anthropic has yet to disclose a target share price for its stock listing.

The company is widely expected to debut with a market valuation of $2 trillion or more, making it the largest stock listing in history. But the figure will be heavily influenced by its financial performance.

Anthropic lost $80.7bn (£60bn) in the first half of this year, double what it lost across 2025 altogether.

The company's overall revenue was $16.2bn billion for the six-month period. Revenues are rising rapidly, but the firm has a long way to go before it breaks even.

Troy Hooper, co-head of equity capital markets at Mergermarket, said Anthropic's revenue growth is "exceptional". But investors are "less forgiving" of tech companies promising huge future returns than they were even months ago, he added.

Anthropic's debt picture is also unclear given it has a huge amount of accounting charges related to certain forms of investment.

"As a result, investors do not yet have a clear view of Anthropic's underlying profitability or whether its rate of cash generation is sufficient to support the business as it scales," Hooper added.

3. But luckily it has plenty of cash on hand

Despite losing money, Anthropic has heaps of cash lying about.

At $131.6bn, almost all of its cash in hand is defined as "working capital", meaning it can use the money to fund its operations day-to-day.

Currently, Anthropic has more cash on hand than Meta and Google combined.

Anthropic's costs could rise as it faces fierce competition for top staff and computing power from other AI giants.

The leasing of data centres alone is costing the company $321.4bn so far this year.

Hooper said such large costs are expected to grow. Even with this kind of cash, it won't be enough to maintain its business growth.

Any investors in Anthropic "will be paying for future dominance, not present-day economics", he said.

4. Anthropic relies on a few big customers

Anthropic sees boundless ways it can sell its technology to customers.

A large portion of its current business comes from just 250 major enterprise customers, which it says have paid it at least $10mn in the past year.

An even smaller number, just five enterprise customers, make up a quarter of its current business.

Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager of Founder ETF, pointed out that "many top Anthropic customers have no long-term contract".

The company's level of business concentration leaves Anthropic dependent on a small fraction of its paying customers to support its growth, with no guarantee it will continue.

Anthropic also has enterprise relationships with the likes of Google and Amazon, both of which are also investors in the company "and competitors", creating potential business conflicts in the future, Monaghan noted.

Anthropic said its overall enterprise customer base has grown rapidly, going from roughly 1,500 customers last year to almost 12,000 this year.

Part of its growth strategy is offering Claude tools for free before working to "convert these users into paying customers over time".

The strategy has led to Claude seeing "the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology in history", the company claimed.

5. AI promises 'extraordinary' benefits to the world

For all of the risks Anthropic has said AI poses, it also reiterated its claim AI will produce an "extraordinary" amount of good.

"Achieving our mission means the world gains the enormous benefits of frontier AI while mitigating the most significant risks," the company said.

That mission is defined as: "The responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity."

"We do not pursue projects based on commercial opportunity or research novelty alone; our efforts must advance our mission. "

Such hypothetical benefits include progress in healthcare, like the development of bespoke treatments for illnesses and improved disease detection, tailored education and legal advice and making more efficient power grids and batteries.

Decades of scientific progress could be condensed into years, accelerating drug discovery, disease detection, and the delivery of personalized therapy.

Anthropic said AI could provide individually tailored education and expert financial and legal advice, advance power grids and battery design for greater efficiency and reliability and help the "developing world" build more technological capabilities.

"Ultimately, we believe frontier AI will help drive global economic growth," the company said.

articles.title: FTC demands Anthropic leaders testify in consumer harm investigation
articles.summary: The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) has asked executives from the AI firm Anthropic to testify as part of its consumer harm probe into the maker of the Claude AI model, a FTC spokesperson confirmed to The Hill on Monday. The demand is part of the consumer protection agency’s larger investigation into Anthropic over the potential…
articles.body:
The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) has asked executives from the AI firm Anthropic to testify as part of its consumer harm probe into the maker of the Claude AI model, a FTC spokesperson confirmed to The Hill on Monday.

The demand is part of the consumer protection agency’s larger investigation into Anthropic over the potential risks their AI models pose to consumers. The agency is also investigating OpenAI, though it did not confirm the same demands were sent to the ChatGPT producer.

The demands, first reported by Axios , come nearly two weeks after the FTC sent subpoenas to OpenAI and Anthropic.

Both companies in recent months have revealed multiple incidents of AI agents accessing other information and data systems without human instruction to do so.

Earlier this month, Anthropic disclosed one of its models submitted a false homicide tip to the Philadelphia Police Department in July. The New York Times also reported this month that Anthropic’s AI agents tried to fill out visa forms on the State Department’s website .

In the wake of recent hacking incidents, leaders from OpenAI and Anthropic have both called for a slowdown of the technology and supported establishing an industry standard on safe technology development.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has tried to set himself apart as an advocate for safer AI development, a position that has caused rifts with the Trump administration in the past.

Earlier Monday, Anthropic filed for its initial public offering to make its historic stock market debut.

The S-1 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission brought the AI firm a step closer to becoming the first large frontier AI lab to go public.

In Monday’s filing, Anthropic highlighted various risks of the technology, including the potential for cyberattacks, design of biological weapons or mass surveillance by government.

articles.title: Elon Musk warns more than 200 AI cloud companies face ‘guppy-level death’ as the AI boom runs into a debt crisis
articles.summary: Musk said that neoclouds could struggle to get financing as lenders grow anxious about AI spending.
articles.body:
Paying for AI infrastructure has strained Silicon Valley's deepest pockets, with even Meta reporting negative $2.1 billion in free cash flow last week as its spending on data centers and chips surged. As investors question whether AI spending will generate enough revenue to justify its costs, the world's richest man offered a grim prediction: Hundreds of smaller companies central to the buildout may not survive.

Elon Musk warned in an X post on Sunday that more than 200 neoclouds, the firms that buy chips and then rent out computing capacity, could face "guppy-level death and consolidation" because lenders are reluctant to finance businesses that depend wholly on AI demand.

"Debt markets have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesn't have substantial revenue independent of AI data centers," Musk wrote . He said SpaceX is exempt from this potential wipeout because it already closed $40 billion in debt financing and has Starlink to generate revenue that's not tethered to AI.

Neoclouds borrow heavily to buy expensive Nvidia chips and build data centers, and then lease out that capacity to model developers. While hyperscalers like Google and Meta have other sources of revenue they can lean on to fuel their AI spending, neoclouds' survival depends on appetite for compute. So if borrowing costs go up or customers cut spending, neoclouds will struggle to pay off their debts.

CoreWeave , one of the biggest neoclouds, illustrates this financial pressure. On one hand, its revenue backlog was $104 billion at the end of the second quarter, with $25 billion in new commitments added early in the third quarter. On the other hand, its latest quarterly filing shows $35.6 billion in outstanding debt at the end of June compared to $5.5 billion in cash and cash equivalents. And last month, CoreWeave took on $4.2 billion more in debt.

Concern about CoreWeave's ability to manage this debt sent the cost of insuring it against default to a record high last week , with credit default swaps implying a more than 60% chance over the next five years.

This is an industry-wide concern. Analysts at research firm Gartner predicted on Oct. 14 that cost pressure and lack of a differentiating business model will force 80% of neoclouds to stop operating by 2030. Data center owners need to make $8.6 trillion in revenue to cover financing costs and capital spending, but enterprise and consumer AI revenue linked to those data centers is forecast at only $3.6 trillion.

Financial markets may represent another limiting factor. Apollo Global Management chief economist Torsten Slok told CNBC there's a "shortage of capital" to fund AI infrastructure because the sector is competing against government debt and deficit financing.

articles.title: Ben Affleck Vs. Nicolas Cage: Why Hollywood’s AI Disagreement Is Good
articles.summary: Affleck sold an AI company to Netflix for $587 million. Cage would rather never work with Amazon again than sign an AI waiver. Between them, Hollywood’s futu...
articles.body:
On Sept. 30, Ben Affleck told the audience at Bloomberg Screentime 2026 that he used generative AI "for lots of things" in his Netflix thriller Animals . On Oct. 10, Nicolas Cage told a New York Comic Con crowd that he had refused to sign a waiver allowing Amazon to use AI on Spider-Noir . Ten days apart, two Oscar winners delivered opposite verdicts on the same technology. The distance between them maps the question Hollywood has been slowly settling: on whose terms generative AI enters the production process.

Ben Affleck and Hollywood's AI Adopters Treat Generative AI As a Tool with Limits

Affleck's position carries weight because he has built a business on it. Netflix paid $587 million in cash for InterPositive , the post-production AI company he founded in 2022, and the streamer has said roughly 300 of its titles have already used generative AI. At Screentime, Affleck dismissed predictions of mass job loss as "propaganda" and called AI "another form of computing." He also said its role on Animals was concentrated in post-production.

His endorsement comes with conditions. He worries about "learned helplessness" in his children's education, and at the film's premiere he said he would not use a model trained on copyrighted work . Nor does he believe a typed prompt will ever produce a movie audiences want to see. Matthew McConaughey occupies similar ground. "It's not coming. It's here," he said of AI at a CNN town hall in February, even as he has reportedly trademarked his image to deter unauthorized imitation.

Nicolas Cage and Other AI Critics Defend Human Authorship and The Jobs Behind It

Cage framed his refusal as a matter of incompatible values. "Amazon is a very AI-friendly company, to the tune of $50 billion invested in OpenAI," he said. "I am not an AI-friendly actor." He added that he is "probably not going to be working with that studio again." Cage did not describe the waiver's terms, and Variety reported the request as an allegation. His preferred alternative is a generation of young directors who, in his words, are "doing it from scratch and by hand."

Resistance isn't confined to actors. Illumination CEO Chris Meledandri said his studio felt no pressure to introduce AI into its pipeline . Meanwhile, SAG-AFTRA reiterated objections to synthetic performer Tilly Norwood, alleging uncompensated use of performers' work. articles.body:
Anthropic publicly filed for an initial public offering (IPO) on Monday morning in what is expected to be a historic stock market debut .

© Markus Schreiber, The Associated Press

The S-1 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) brings the Claude maker a step closer to becoming the first large frontier AI lab to go public. It is expected to be a major test for investors’ interest in the technology.

The stock will trade under the ticker ANT on the Nasdaq exchange, according to the filing, and could happen as soon as November .

The filing showed Anthropic’s revenue has drastically jumped in the past year, yet the company reported a net loss of $80.7 billion in the first half of this year. The company was valued earlier this year at $965 billion by private investors, The Associated Press reported.

It comes as AI safety concerns dominate headlines , following various security breaches and warnings from executives including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about the technology’s risks to society .

In Monday’s filing, Anthropic highlighted various risks of the technology , including the potential for cyberattacks, design of biological weapons or mass surveillance by government.

“We consider it our personal responsibility to help the world understand these risks, to prevent or mitigate them when they arise from our AI models, and to work with governments and the rest of the industry to address them at a societal level,” the company wrote.

Anthropic confidentially filed paperwork with the SEC in early June, though no other details were released at the time. A week later, rival AI company OpenAI also confidentially filed to go public , though it is not clear when the ChatGPT maker will take the next step.

Anthropic’s IPO could be the largest in history, beating the record recently set by E lon Musk’s SpaceX last June, in which shares opened at $150.

articles.title: Anthropic is burning gas to feed the AI boom
articles.summary: Anthropic’s IPO filing shows us how dependent data centers are on gas, even as climate change poses financial risks.
articles.body: As it prepares to go public, Anthropic’s S-1 filing makes generative AI’s methane dependency glaringly obvious. In documents filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission Monday, Anthropic acknowledges that data centers are becoming increasingly reliant on “natural gas” — the fossil fuel industry’s marketing term for what is primarily methane — leaving the company’s AI data center buildout vulnerable to rising fuel costs and existing supply chain constraints. And in a possible catch-22, Anthropic admits that rising global temperatures — a symptom of burning fossil fuels — will increase the company’s operating costs. “Competition for access to electrical supply and data center locations with adequate power availability is intense,” Anthropic says, adding that some of its planned data centers rely on electricity generated by natural gas turbines on-site. Anthropic leases capacity from hyperscalers, but it announced a $50 billion dollar plan last year to expand data centers in Texas and New York. The US, the epicenter for data centers globally, is planning to build more fossil fuel generation capacity than it has in a decade as data centers demand more electricity. Donald Trump’s administration has sought to kill renewable energy projects while tilting the regulatory landscape in favor of fossil fuels, which Trump claims is a more important energy source for powering data centers around the clock than solar and wind farms that generate power intermittently. Now, a shortage of gas turbines is slowing data center construction. Some developers are installing gas engines on-site as a way to avoid long wait times to connect to power grids. Developers are also turning to more simple turbine technology at these sites as they face backlogs from turbine manufacturers, making on-site power generation less efficient and more polluting as a result. Data center electricity demand could wipe out decades of gains in air quality over the next five years, one recent Texas-based study found — raising levels of soot, smog-forming pollutants, and planet-heating carbon dioxide. Even as data centers create more greenhouse gas pollution, Anthropic’s S-1 points to climate change as a risk to its bottom line. It will have to pay more for electricity and water to cool servers at data centers as temperatures climb. Nevertheless, Anthropic expects increased competition for natural gas and pipeline capacity from hyperscalers and cloud service providers rushing to build their own data centers. “This competition could drive up the price of natural gas,” the company notes. Gas makes up the biggest chunk of the US electricity mix, 40 percent of the nation’s power generation. And Americans are already feeling the pain of rising costs as utilities scramble to upgrade energy infrastructure and meet rising power demand. Pissed-off residents have successfully blocked dozens of proposed data centers across the US. Anthropic acknowledges that the specter of ballooning utility bills is enough to interfere with a data center project. “If our efforts to secure electrical power are perceived to affect other utility customers and the broader grid, regulators may impose conditions, standby charges, or other requirements intended to address such impacts,” it says. If regulators push data center developers to shoulder more of the costs for new energy infrastructure, Anthropic says that could also raise its operating costs. And without a secure gas supply and the pipelines to transport the fuel, the company says, it might need to delay or abandon planned data center projects altogether. Ultimately, these challenges could stunt Anthropic’s growth: > Any failure to secure access to adequate electrical power, any legal, regulatory, or other administrative action or change limiting the availability of electricity, or any significant increase in energy or compliance costs, could adversely affect our cost structure and limit our ability to scale our compute infrastructure, develop and deploy our models, and service our customers.

articles.title: OpenAI announces three big science discoveries and a new way to work with academics
articles.summary: OpenAI says its models have produced three new discoveries including proving the Exponential Time Hypothesis is false.
articles.body: Less than a month after its mass release of hundreds of manuscripts that it said contained solutions to long-standing mathematics questions, OpenAI is back with three more “major” discoveries in math, computer science, and physics. What’s different this time is the choice to have external experts that OpenAI describes as “shepherds” guiding the results in computer science and physics, while for the math problem it says that they advised it to release the AI output for researchers to work through their own explanations. > OpenAI results added to GitHub today: > Local smoothing for the Euclidean wave equation. The proof uses an auxiliary partial differential equation to establish Sogge’s local smoothing for waves in every spatial dimension at least two. It also yields the Kakeya maximal and dimension conjectures and Stein’s spherical restriction estimates throughout the interior of the conjectured range. We are releasing the model output directly, as we did in our October 6 release. > The Exponential Time Hypothesis is False. The paper gives a deterministic algorithm that exactly counts satisfying assignments of fixed-width CNF formulas in subexponential time and polynomial space. The case of 3-SAT refutes the Exponential Time Hypothesis. An independent working group of computer scientists led by Russell Impagliazzo, Ramamohan Paturi, and Ryan Williams will examine and explain the proof. At the group’s request, we are making the materials public immediately so others can examine them as well. This approach could have its own issues, the company admits, and the AGMAI panel of math advisers OpenAI put together just said yesterday that “we recommend that AI companies do not adopt” the practices of designating certain people to receive the output first, citing unequal access, borrowed reputation, and biased selection as a few of the issues. Instead, they recommended that in the future, AI labs release output on scholarly repositories, with Lean-formalized proofs, info on how the problems were chosen, funding for people working on understanding the results, and other information. The physics information has not been released in full, but is a “mathematically rigorous existence proof of certain interacting quantum field theories containing gauge fields and fermions in four dimensions, including Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) and a unified completion of the Standard Model of particle physics.” According to OpenAI, “David Gross will lead a group including Michael Douglas, Arthur Jaffe, Igor Klebanov, and Nikita Nekrasov that will shepherd this work.” The computer science collaboration is said to prove that the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), which has been widely believed to be true, is actually false. OpenAI says verification of the result will be guided by a group of three experts that includes UC San Diego’s Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi, who were part of the group that originally proposed it in 1999, as well as MIT professor Ryan Williams. The group decided to release the AI output write-up and Lean proof on GitHub today. They also released an open letter to the community asking for input on how to examine the claim, and about setting norms for dealing with AI-generated breakthroughs: > We would welcome discussion of three broader questions: > What expectations should govern early access to AI-generated results, disclosure of conflicts of interest, and the use of unpublished material for subsequent research? > How should credit recognize both new discoveries and the work of checking, fixing, simplifying, explaining, and extending them? > How can we support students and researchers as methods and research directions change, while preserving the understanding and judgment needed to question results and develop new ideas? There’s similar documentation for the math breakthrough, where its model “produced a proof of the local smoothing conjecture in every dimension and therefore also resolve the Kakeya conjecture and Stein’s restriction conjecture in all dimensions.” Just a few months ago, NYU professor Hong Wang was awarded a prestigious Fields Medal by the International Mathematical Union for resolving the Kakeya conjecture in three dimensions.

articles.title: Empresas recorrem à religião para ensinar ética à IA | G1
articles.standfirst: Gigantes da tecnologia consultam líderes religiosos e filósofos em busca de princípios para orientar seus modelos, mas especialistas alertam para os limites dessa abordagem.
articles.summary: Gigantes da tecnologia consultam líderes religiosos e filósofos em busca de princípios para orientar seus modelos, mas especialistas alertam para os limites dessa abordagem.
articles.body:
Sigla em inglês para inteligência artificial. — Foto: Aly Song/Reuters

Enquanto empresas de tecnologia competem para desenvolver a inteligência artificial mais poderosa, algumas também se perguntam como ensinar um chatbot a distinguir o certo do errado . A resposta? A religião.

“Essas não são perguntas que um laboratório possa responder”, disse Chris Olah, cofundador da Anthropic, no início deste ano, durante a apresentação, no Vaticano , da encíclica do Papa Leão XIV sobre inteligência artificial. “São perguntas com as quais tradições como a sua lidam há milênios.”

Em meio a essa tão discutida aproximação com a fé, houve pouca atenção pública ao que exatamente essas empresas de tecnologia entendem por religião — e, talvez mais importante, ao que esperam obter com essa aproximação.

Enquanto executivos alertam para o potencial destrutivo da IA e debatem a necessidade de desenvolver modelos capazes de tomar decisões alinhadas a determinados princípios morais , recorrem cada vez mais a filósofos e líderes religiosos.

A ideia pode ser resumida assim: a religião ajudaria a orientar o desenvolvimento da IA em um ambiente no qual os temores em torno da tecnologia — fundamentados ou não — se espalham pela sociedade.

Como essas empresas não estão vinculadas a uma religião específica, o objetivo costuma ser bastante amplo: encontrar um conjunto de princípios morais capaz de orientar seus modelos. “O que eu acho que o ChatGPT deveria fazer é refletir essa média ponderada, ou algo assim, da visão moral da humanidade”, disse Sam Altman, CEO da OpenAI , no ano passado.

Mas especialistas e praticantes de diferentes religiões alertam que essa ideia não leva em conta o fato de que tradições e visões de mundo podem se contradizer. Em resumo, dizem eles, não é exatamente assim que a religião funciona.

Religião é mais do que um conjunto de regras

Há décadas, estudiosos contestam a visão amplamente difundida da religião como um conjunto de regras ou princípios que podem ser separados das maneiras “complicadas, práticas e improvisadas” pelas quais os fiéis vivem sua fé, afirma Webb Keane, antropólogo da Universidade de Michigan.

A ideia de que a religião pode ser separada de áreas como a cultura e a política permanece arraigada, embora, na prática, esteja profundamente ligada a ambas.

Alguns temem que as empresas de IA, ao recorrerem a líderes religiosos para responder a questões éticas, reforcem uma concepção de religião que não reconhece plenamente a importância da doutrina, dos rituais e das relações entre seus praticantes.

Eis a questão, argumenta Keane: se partirmos do pressuposto de que a religião pode oferecer um conjunto isolável de princípios morais, usá-la para treinar sistemas de IA pode acabar priorizando certas tradições e distorcendo outras — especialmente aquelas que não se definem primordialmente como sistemas éticos.

“Existe uma maneira muito convencional de pensar na religião como um livro de regras”, disse ele. “Certamente, isso está muito ligado à religião bíblica e, no fim das contas, às religiões abraâmicas.”

Empresas buscam ampliar o diálogo com religiosos

Isso não significa que essas reuniões tenham faltado diversidade. Tampouco quer dizer que o envolvimento das empresas com a religião tenha sido pouco cuidadoso, na avaliação de participantes como Meghan Sullivan, filósofa da religião que lidera uma iniciativa sobre ética e IA na Universidade de Notre Dame.

Embora não enumere as tradições consultadas, a Anthropic afirmou, em uma publicação de maio em seu blog, que se reuniu com “acadêmicos, clérigos, filósofos e especialistas em ética de mais de 15 grupos religiosos e interculturais” — grupo que pretende ampliar no futuro.

No início deste ano, Sullivan participou de uma reunião da Anthropic que contou com cristãos de diferentes denominações.

Em comparação com conversas que teve com outras empresas de tecnologia, ela disse ter ficado impressionada com a profundidade com que a Anthropic abordou questões religiosas. A empresa é amplamente reconhecida por dar especial atenção à ética e à segurança da IA.

“A cultura dentro da empresa é semelhante à de um bom campus universitário, no sentido de que há um grupo de pessoas muito curiosas intelectualmente”, disse ela. “Essas reuniões são bem nerds — não sei se essa é a melhor maneira de descrever —, no bom sentido.”

A reunião foi dividida em duas partes. Primeiro, a empresa explicou seus modelos “em termos simples” aos participantes. Em seguida, os líderes religiosos fizeram comentários e debateram as questões apresentadas, segundo Sullivan.

“Discutimos todo tipo de questão moral que essa tecnologia levanta — desde ‘Será que os humanos têm alma?’ até ‘Alunos do terceiro ano deveriam ter acesso a um chatbot para ajudar na alfabetização?’”

Representantes da Meta, do Google e da Amazon também se reuniram com representantes do Vaticano, enquanto a Microsoft tem ampliado sua atuação junto a comunidades religiosas.

A religião é geralmente considerada antiga e universal. Embora estudiosos como o falecido e influente Jonathan Z. Smith reconheçam que isso é verdade em alguns aspectos, eles argumentam que essa visão não conta toda a história.

“O homem teve toda a sua história para imaginar divindades e modos de interação com elas. Mas o homem, mais precisamente o homem ocidental, teve apenas os últimos séculos para imaginar a religião”, escreveu Smith em 1982.

Muitos estudiosos da religião hoje compartilham a visão de Smith. Eles questionam a ideia de que as religiões formam um conjunto de sistemas distintos e comparáveis e argumentam que essa é uma concepção moderna, que remonta ao século XIX.

O budismo e o hinduísmo, por exemplo, não eram reconhecidos como tradições claramente delimitadas pelas populações que os praticavam antes da chegada de estudiosos europeus, afirma Tomoko Masuzawa, estudiosa da religião e autora de “A Invenção das Religiões Mundiais”. “Todas essas categorias não eram nativas”, acrescenta.

Acadêmicos ocidentais consolidaram essas categorias ao longo dos anos e só começaram a reexaminá-las de forma mais sistemática na segunda metade do século XX.

Essas ideias arraigadas sobre religião — entre elas, a noção de que tradições religiosas podem ser facilmente comparadas entre diferentes culturas — ajudam a explicar por que o Vale do Silício pode não sentir necessidade de definir o que entende por religião.

Na tentativa de representar diferentes pontos de vista, recorrer à religião acaba se tornando uma maneira aparentemente simples de incorporar diversidade de pensamento.

“De alguma forma, a religião se torna uma maneira de mapear o mundo”, disse Masuzawa. “É como se o mundo inteiro tivesse aderido a ela.”

Ao reunir diferentes visões, IA pode apagar particularidades

Alguns especialistas defendem que as empresas definam com mais clareza seus termos e objetivos, para que seja possível entender exatamente o que esperam obter desse diálogo com a religião.

“Este trabalho não busca alinhar nossos modelos à visão de mundo de uma tradição específica. Queremos que Claude se inspire em uma ampla gama de pontos de vista — religiosos, seculares e políticos — com igual profundidade e rigor”, afirmou a Anthropic na publicação. “O que buscamos nessas conversas é uma reflexão cuidadosa e acumulada sobre como o bom caráter realmente se forma.”

Os grandes modelos de linguagem geram textos prevendo, sucessivamente, quais elementos têm maior probabilidade de aparecer em seguida, a partir de padrões identificados durante seu treinamento em grandes volumes de conteúdo produzido por humanos, incluindo textos religiosos.

Paolo Carozza, membro do Conselho de Supervisão independente da Meta e especialista jurídico em pensamento social católico e tecnologia, teme que, ao combinar diferentes perspectivas, as características que definem determinada tradição acabem se perdendo. Na prática, diz ele, elas poderiam ser homogeneizadas, produzindo uma visão mais genérica ou que privilegie tradições religiosas ocidentais.

“Qualquer tradição viva e sofisticada é capaz, ao longo do tempo, de interagir com outras tradições, absorver novos conhecimentos e evoluir. Mas faz isso de forma orgânica”, disse ele. “O que a IA, acredito, muitas vezes faz — ou pode fazer — não ocorre de forma orgânica. Ela simplesmente mistura tudo, desorganiza tudo e, assim, acaba não dando sentido a nada.”

articles.title: Alunos usam IA para monitorar insetos e biodiversidade no PI | G1
articles.standfirst: A iniciativa monitora polinizadores e insetos bioindicadores com a ajuda de estudantes, professores e moradores para acompanhar mudanças ambientais na região de Guaribas.
articles.summary: A iniciativa monitora polinizadores e insetos bioindicadores com a ajuda de estudantes, professores e moradores para acompanhar mudanças ambientais na região de Guaribas.
articles.body:
Alunos usam IA para monitorar insetos que ajudam a preservar biodiversidade no PI — Foto: Divulgação/Seduc

Alunos do Centro Estadual de Tempo Integral (Ceti) Paulo Freire, em Guaribas , no Sul do Piauí, desenvolveram um projeto que une conhecimentos de biologia e Inteligência Artificial (IA) para contribuir com a preservação de organismos essenciais ao equilíbrio ambiental e à produção rural.

O projeto nomeado de PolinizAI, funciona como um monitor de polinizadores e de insetos bioindicadores, como os vaga-lumes . Os estudantes participam de atividades de campo, registram fotografias, catalogam informações e coletam depoimentos de moradores e agricultores mais antigos da região.

🔎 Os insetos bioindicadores refletem condições específicas de um ecossistema, como poluição e degradação, devido à sensibilidade a estresses ambientais.

“Com a IA desplugada, trabalhamos a organização e a comparação desses dados para compreender padrões. O conteúdo da sala de aula se conecta com o que eles observam sobre o lugar onde vivem”, explica a professora Amanda Sousa.

Segundo a Secretaria de Estado da Educação do Piauí (Seduc), o projeto nasceu da necessidade de moradores da região compreenderem melhor as mudanças climáticas e ambientais observadas .

Após a conclusão do levantamento, a equipe pretende desenvolver um site para que estudantes, professores e agricultores possam continuar monitorando e acompanhando os registros da biodiversidade da região.

“A ideia do site é reunir o que estamos pesquisando e facilitar o acesso a essas informações. Queremos que ele ajude outras pessoas a conhecer os polinizadores da região e a acompanhar os registros, para que o trabalho continue e também seja útil à comunidade”, explicou a estudante Fernanda Maia.

articles.title: Cohere says Alibaba’s Qwen model tried to send a file to Beijing | TechCrunch
articles.summary: An AI model said it wouldn’t use any tools, then tried to send something to a server in Beijing anyway, and while researchers say it’s probably a training quirk and not espionage, the whole thing has people asking how much to trust free Chinese AI.
articles.body:
Canadian AI company Cohere said on Monday that it found one of Alibaba’s newest AI models, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, trying to upload a file to a server in Beijing during a routine cybersecurity test, even though the model had said in its own notes that it wouldn’t use any tools.

The incident initially raised fears that the model had undermined a fundamental promise to businesses — that self-hosting an open-weight model keeps data in-house. But those early fears of corporate espionage were short-lived. Researchers quickly dismissed the threat, saying it was likely a byproduct of messy training environments that cause models to unexpectedly act outside their instructions rather than a deliberate attempt to secretly send sensitive information to China.

The incident began on Friday during an evaluation in which the Qwen model was asked to write a rule for catching malware downloads. According to a blog post from Cohere, the model’s written reasoning explicitly stated it would not use any external tools. Yet in the very next step, it attempted to send a test string (a short piece of placeholder text) to an external server before being blocked by a security sandbox.

Cohere said it could not tell whether the behavior was deliberate or a leftover from its training.

Asked about the debate over the model’s intent, Cohere co-founder Ivan Zhang told TechCrunch that Cohere has seen its own models pick up strange habits in training simulators.

“It’s really hard to assign intention or motivation. We’ve read our own model traces, we’ve seen reward hacks, and sometimes these models get really creative when it comes to trying to break out their sandboxes,” Zhang said. (Reward hacks are shortcuts a model finds to earn credit without doing a task as intended.)

To teach an AI model to act as an agent that takes actions on its own, companies like Alibaba train it in thousands of practice setups, sort of like flight simulators for software. The model is rewarded every time it finishes a task in a simulator, and it picks up habits along the way. If these practice setups routinely stored files on Alibaba’s cloud servers, models could learn to save files there by default.

Critics also argued that the incident could have been caused by the way Cohere investigated the behavior, steering the model toward it instead of measuring how often Qwen does it on its own.

To find what triggered the upload attempt, Cohere supplied the beginning of a network command (an instruction telling one computer to connect to another) and let the model finish it. Because it processed thousands of routine network commands during its training, the model acted like a highly advanced autocomplete — often filling in web addresses, some of them for Alibaba’s servers.

Cohere said the original upload attempt happened without any such help, but that the behavior is rare.

After developers asked for more evidence, Cohere released the raw traces from its tests on Monday evening on the AI developer platform Hugging Face, along with a script so others could try to reproduce the behavior.

One initial skeptic, after going through the traces, rated the evidence as strong that Qwen can invent suspicious web addresses, but found no evidence that Alibaba planted a backdoor or that Qwen was deliberately hiding its intent.

The incident lands as governments are deciding how far to push back on Chinese AI. Last week, the Department of Homeland Security ordered federal civilian agencies to remove the Chinese AI developer DeepSeek’s products from their systems.

In its blog post, Cohere called on governments to clarify whether their restrictions on Chinese AI also apply to models running on government computers

“I’m not asking for full regulation of these open weights models,” Zhang told TechCrunch, adding that companies should treat open models like any program downloaded from the internet.

Cohere, which sells its own AI models to governments, stands to benefit if officials grow warier of free Chinese alternatives.

articles.title: How OpenAI turned its coding tools into dots, an always-on personal assistant | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Alexander Embiricos, the OpenAI executive responsible for dots, never wants to have a meeting with someone else's AI agent.
articles.body:
The always-on AI personal assistant, which keeps working in the background even when you aren’t asking it to, is this year’s answer to the question of how people will actually use deep learning models. The startup Instinct became an overnight sensation, and Meta put the full force of its marketing behind its assistant, Muse.

OpenAI wasn’t going to be left out. The company released dots , its assistant offering, at its developer day in late September. Alexander Embiricos, who leads OpenAI’s enterprise product team, joined us at TechCrunch Disrupt this month to explain where the product came from—starting with the question of why so many companies seem to be turning to cutesy mascots as avatars for their trillion-parameter matrix multiplication machines.

“There’s kind of this convergent evolution happening,” Embiricos said of the efforts to build AI assistants. “As we were working on the product, we realized if we could frame this as, it’s an entity and it’s a single conversation, not many different conversations….it starts to become intuitive.”

The assistant is available in the ChatGPT desktop and mobile apps to subscribers on the Pro tier or higher, with plans starting at $100 a month. Once it is connected to your calendar, email, computer and other tools, the agent tries to help you get your work done.

Embiricos points out that you could achieve much of dots’ functionality with Open AI’s Codex app, its coding tool, released at the beginning of this year. But that requires more work and hand-holding. He recalled celebrating when his wife started leaving her computer on all night so that her agents could keep working.

“On the product team, what I think about is, how do we make this intuitive and useful to people?” he told Disrupt attendees. “A lot of that isn’t building some new piece of tech into the product; it’s how you frame it to the user and how it feels.”

The path from chat bot to coding tool to personal assistant

Making the technology feel intuitive meant repackaging the functionality of the company’s models into something more accessible, a path it was already on as it spun ChatGPT Work out of the agentic coding tools it had built for software engineers. Even the name—a play on the negative space inside of OpenAI’s logo—is intended “to feel like just something that could eventually be ubiquitous.” (Asked when he learned that rival AI entrepreneur Elon Musk owns the dot.com URL, Embiricos said, “I found out very late.”)

The idea of a persistent agent is that it doesn’t need prompting. For OpenAI, means more token usage, and for users, a more pro-active assistant “that’s sort of thinking about you and thinking how to help you,” as Embiricos put it.

In our testing, the assistant’s ability to think ahead is apparent and often useful, but it isn’t quite there yet. It will flag calendar conflicts and upcoming deadlines, but not necessarily in the most timely fashion.

“The first time it told me about one of those [conflicts]—this is like early in development—it told me three minutes before the thing,” Embiricos says of his dot. “It’s like, ‘Hey, this thing is coming up. You might want to do something about it.’ I only have three minutes!”

Embiricos expects the timing to improve over time, but the proactive approach is key to the product. “I was hearing about an engineer at a drone delivery startup, and they were saying, ‘We had this outage, and by the time I noticed that the outage was going on, my dot had already noticed the outage was happening, had already analyzed the outage, and had come to me with useful information for how we could resolve the outage.’”

As with most AI agent use cases, there’s a tension between the personal information an AI model needs to be useful and exactly how much personal data you are exposing to a software company. Muse has been criticized for the profiles it builds of your family and friends, which the software uses to know, say, what kind of restaurant you might want to go to with a specific pal, but could also add incredible value to Meta’s advertising business. Does dots collect similar data?

“Yes, we have a thing that we built into dots, which we call proactive research,” Embiricos said. “On a cadence, it will think about what it knows about you, what is the conversation that it’s had, and then what have you given it access to that it can think about, and then it will go and research, ‘What could I do to be more helpful to you?’ And then, basically, it will propose that.”

It’s difficult to separate the data needs of the agent from that of its parent corporation. Hark, a start-up developing its own AI personal assistant, is explicit in pointing out it that it doesn’t collect data to fuel an advertising business the way that OpenAI and Meta do.

With dots, OpenAI says that the agent has the same privacy controls as ChatGPT itself: Users can turn off model training (stopping OpenAI from using their conversations to improve its AI), and control what resources it accesses within your computer and how. Still, those controls aren’t granular and the app can be pushy. For example, it refuses to accept read-only access to cloud drives.

“What I think we need to do is basically build out super, super, super granular controls,” Embiricos said, but he pointed to the model’s intelligence and discretion as the other side of this coin.

“This is actually something we kind of got some flack about when we launched,” Embiricos said. “We had really conservative defaults over what the agent would do, and it would ask for permission a lot. I remember knowing that we were going to see that feedback, but thinking, ‘This is okay, we can tune that over time.’”

The other big question about AI agents is whether they can scale. They’re fun when only a few people have them, and stories of agents snagging hard-to-get reservations abound. But businesses don’t necessarily like dealing with agents and might not be equipped to. People certainly don’t like dealing with them (note: stop having your AI agents pitch me), and Embiricos is among those people. He also has a human assistant because OpenAI’s corporate partners want to interact with a person, he said, adding, “I personally never intend to have a meeting with someone else’s agent.”

If the AI industry is right that agents are our future, can we get there without overwhelming the infrastructure that our world currently runs on, from businesses and websites to payment networks?

“At OpenAI…we’re not always moving the fastest in terms of shipping the next ability for the agent to work with the world,” he said. “When we do, we’re doing it really closely in collaboration with the rest of the ecosystem. I probably can’t say too much here, but we’re deep in lots of conversations with payment processors.”

Letting an AI assistant spend money through partnerships with payment companies would be a potentially lucrative first for OpenAI, but also a big ask for consumers. Giving an assistant access to my email inbox already feels like a big ask, but my bank account is off limits. For now.

articles.title: Remote work automation just crossed a troubling threshold
articles.summary: The important lesson is not that humans are obsolete; it is that the automation rate on real freelance work has risen from near-floor performance to a level businesses can no longer dismiss.
articles.body:
The newest Remote Labor Index results suggest that digital labor automation is moving from toy tasks toward real client work — the kind with messy files, vague briefs, visual judgment, hidden defects, and a paying customer waiting at the end.

That does not mean artificial intelligence has conquered professional work. It does mean that the line between “impressive assistant” and “partial worker” is shifting faster than many executives, policymakers or workers are prepared to admit.

This result delivers an especially sharp warning for the labor market because the Remote Labor Index asks a harder question than most on AI. Instead of testing whether models can solve puzzles, answer exam questions or produce plausible text, the index evaluates whether AI systems can complete end-to-end freelance projects across fields such as architecture, graphic design, video, audio, data analysis and web apps. The output is compared with professional human work, and the core question is brutally practical: Would a client accept the AI deliverable?

That standard changes the conversation altogether.

A chatbot that can explain architecture is not the same as one that can produce a dimensioned floor plan from scanned documents and photos. A model that can generate beautiful images is not the same as one that can build a usable 3D file. A system that can draft code is not the same as one that can ship a functioning web app under constraints. This is why real-world benchmarks are becoming the only honest way to talk about AI and work.

The latest numbers are still modest, but the trajectory is not. The Center for AI Safety reports that the best system at the benchmark’s launch automated 2.5 percent of projects. But by July 2026 update, newer frontier systems had reached much higher rates. Fable 5 reported at 16 percent (with caveats); Opus 4.8 was automating at 8 percent; and GPT-5.5 at 6 percent.

The important lesson is not that humans are obsolete, but that the automation rate on real freelance work has risen from near-floor performance to a level that businesses can no longer dismiss.

The examples reveal why this is both exciting and dangerous. The systems can generate work that looks close to professional at first glance. Yet the defects often sit below the surface.

A rendering may look polished even as the underlying 3D model is malformed. An animation may be smoother than earlier generations but still miss the standard a client is paying for. A floor plan may look increasingly accurate while still requiring professional correction. The machine’s output is no longer obviously useless, yet that makes it both more useful and more risky at the same time.

That is why human evaluation remains central.

OpenAI’s GDPval work highlights the difficulty of judging professional deliverables with automated graders. When evaluation depends on taste, domain expertise, file inspection and tool use, the grader faces the same problem as the worker — it must understand not just whether something looks good, but also whether it functions, whether it satisfies the brief, and whether hidden flaws would impose costs later.

This is the practical meaning of the jagged frontier . AI can outperform humans on some hard-looking tasks while failing at work that a skilled professional finds routine. Stanford’s 2026 AI Index notes that AI capability is accelerating, yet it also points to uneven performance across benchmarks and real-world task execution. That unevenness is exactly what employers will experience: stunning shortcuts in one workflow, baffling failures in the next, and a constant need to decide where human judgment has to stay in the loop.

The labor question therefore cannot be reduced to “Will AI replace jobs?” The better question is which tasks become cheaper, which workflows become reorganized, and which workers become responsible for supervising machine output.

The International Labor Organization’s 2025 update on occupational exposure treats generative AI as a task-level force, not a simple job-killing machine. That is the right frame. Work changes first at the edges, through handoffs, reviews, templates, drafts, prototypes and partial deliverables.

Adoption data points in the same direction. Anthropic’s research on actual AI use shows a gap between what models might theoretically do and what people actually delegate to them. Its June 2026 Economic Index report also finds that AI use reflects the rhythms of work and produces concrete artifacts such as documents, explanations, code and reports through increasingly autonomous interfaces. That makes AI agents less like a novelty and more like a new layer of workplace infrastructure.

For executives, the mistake is to treat this as a procurement problem. Buying access to stronger models will not automatically produce stronger organizations. The Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development’s review of AI productivity gains emphasizes that results depend on the task, the user’s experience, and the quality of human-AI collaboration. In plain English, productivity comes from redesigned workflows, better verification and employees who know when to trust the machine and when to challenge it.

For workers, the mistake is to treat today’s limitations as permanent shelter. A 16 percent automation rate is not a revolution by itself. But a quadrupling in under a year is a signal. If AI can do one slice of a freelance project today, it may do three slices tomorrow. The durable skill is no longer mere production. It is defining the brief, detecting defects, integrating tools, communicating tradeoffs, and owning the final judgment.

The most sensible corporate response is neither blind automation nor defensive denial. Leaders need a future of work operating model that treats AI as a junior producer with unusual speed, uneven competence and no accountability. Give it constrained work, require inspection, track defects, and compare cost savings against review time. Reward employees for catching its failures — not just for producing more output.

That shift also requires a more mature culture of responsible AI adoption . Companies should stop asking whether a model can create a deliverable and start asking whether the organization can safely accept it. Who checks the file? Who signs off? Who explains the limitation to the client? Who owns the error when the render looks right but the model is wrong?

Digital labor automation is no longer a distant forecast; it is an uneven, measurable, accelerating capability. The future will not arrive as a clean replacement of humans by machines. It will arrive as a thousand acceptance decisions, one deliverable at a time. The organizations that win will be the ones that learn to measure those decisions before the market measures them instead.

Gleb Tsipursky, Ph.D., serves as the CEO of the future-of-work consultancy Disaster Avoidance Experts and wrote “ The Psychology of AI Adoption at Work: From Resistance to Results ” and “ ChatGPT for Leaders and Content Creators .”

articles.title: General Compute raises $100 million Series A, countering the neocloud disaster narrative | TechCrunch
articles.summary: General Compute is betting on inference chips from outside the Nvidia ecosystem.
articles.body:
CoreWeave, a publicly traded neocloud that rents out computing power for AI, has seen its stock price fall to a 12-month low, and Elon Musk is flexing $40 billion in debt for buying computing capacity and predicting that “200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation.” It’s not exactly the ideal week to announce a Series A for a neocloud.

General Compute co-founder and CEO Finn Puklowski is unfazed. He’s bullish on CoreWeave’s chances, and thinks Musk is just talking his book to drive down the prices of the GPUs he wants to buy. Fears of a chip-led collapse are “massively overstated. I have people calling me up every single week asking me to do TPUs, GPUs, any chip, to get them more compute.”

Just as important, he says, Anthropic’s bullish S-1 is “settling fears for today.”

General Compute has found a niche building its cloud out of specialized inference chips built by Nvidia rivals. The company struck a $400 million deal to purchase new chips from SambaNova—the first debt financing of inference chips—and now has added Positron and Cerebras to its portfolio of chip suppliers.

A deal with a large customer worth $100 million in annual recurring revenue has paved the way for the company to raise $100 million in Series A funding led by Blackbird Ventures and Abstract Ventures. Valued at $60 million after a May seed round , General Compute is now worth $800 million post-money to its investors.

The startup’s strategy is to zig where others zag. It focused on chips built for inference while everyone else chased GPUs. And instead of taking on a complex effort to build huge data centers, it uses smaller power sources, rents space in other companies’ data centers, and converts former bitcoin-mining sites into places that run AI models.

That approach means General Compute isn’t going to catapult into the top ranks of neoclouds or compete with hyperscalers any time soon. But it’s also not subject to the constraints that come with building data centers from scratch. When General Compute has chips, it will have someplace to plug them in. Puklowski expects the company to deploy 75 megawatts of computing capacity in 2027, and he suspects he will have access to 200 megawatts of power—“more than we can probably fund and get hardware for.”

Still, the plan has a limit. Puklowski’s financing work isn’t done—”capital is going to be a full-time job for me, both on debt and equity,” he told TechCrunch.

The startup has found key customers in cloud companies that specialize in offering developers high-speed inference; General Compute provides the bare metal, or raw servers with no software layered on top, for them to bring their offerings to market. James Palmer, a principal at Blackbird who co-led the round, said his firm’s confidence in General Compute comes in part from an investment in Baseten, an inference cloud company.

“We’ve been proximate to their journey over the last 10 months and observing the wild growth story that [Baseten] has gone on, and the demand for open weight inference, and for companies owning their own intelligence,” Palmer told TechCrunch. When it comes to General Compute, he said, “Cerebras, Positron, SambaNova, all need distribution partners who can take them to scale, who can navigate the complexity of the physical world.”

Executives at all three chipmakers sang General Compute’s praises to TechCrunch, each noting the importance of the company’s focus on making the economics of AI cloud compute work. “Everyone in this market is selling speed,” Rodrigo Liang, SambaNova’s CEO and co-founder, said. “The real question is whether you can make money doing it.”
